title: Do Old Stumps Attract Termites and Carpenter Ants?
meta_title: Do Stumps Attract Termites in Iowa? | OnlyStumps
meta_description: A rotting stump is exactly what carpenter ants and termites look for. What actually moves in, how close to the house is too close, and when to worry.
lede: Yes. A decaying stump is damp, soft, and full of cellulose, which is close to ideal for carpenter ants and eastern subterranean termites. Whether it becomes your problem depends mostly on distance.
excerpt: Yes. A rotting stump is close to ideal habitat. How close to the house is too close, and what actually moves in.

sections.heading: What actually moves into a stump
paragraphs: Carpenter ants are the most common. They do not eat wood, they tunnel through it to nest, and they strongly prefer wood that has already softened with moisture. A stump that has been sitting a couple of years is exactly that.

Eastern subterranean termites matter more. They live in soil and feed on wood in contact with it, which describes a stump perfectly. They are far less visible than ants, and by the time you notice them they have usually been there a while.

sections.heading: Why the stump is not really the problem
paragraphs: A colony in a stump at the back of a two-acre lot is not doing you any harm. The concern is proximity. A colony is a foraging base, and workers range outward from it looking for more wood.

The rough guideline is that a rotting stump within about 20 feet of your foundation, deck posts, or a wood-sided outbuilding is worth removing on those grounds alone. Closer than 10 feet and it should be a priority.

sections.heading: Signs something has already set up
paragraphs: Coarse sawdust that looks like pencil shavings piled at the base usually means carpenter ants. So do large black ants trailing to and from the stump at dusk.
Termites leave mud tubes, which are pencil-width earth tunnels running up the side of the wood. You may also find the wood is soft and layered when you kick it, with soil packed into the galleries.
Either way, grinding removes the nesting site but does not by itself end an established colony. If you are seeing mud tubes near the house, get a pest control company involved as well.

sections.heading: Grinding versus leaving it to rot
paragraphs: A stump left alone in eastern Iowa takes anywhere from five to fifteen years to break down, depending on species and how wet the site stays. Oak and walnut sit there a long time.
That whole window is habitat. Grinding takes the trunk out in an afternoon and turns the remaining root mass into something that rots quietly underground without offering an easy nest above it.

sections.heading: What to do with the chips
paragraphs: Fresh grindings are not much of an attractant on their own. They dry out fast and are too fine to nest in. Still, if the stump was close to the house, have them hauled rather than mounded against the foundation.
Our cleanup add-on takes the grindings away, and the landscape restoration option backfills the hole with topsoil, which leaves nothing sitting against the siding.

faqs.q: Will grinding a stump get rid of the ants?
faqs.a: It removes the nest site, which usually scatters them. An established colony that has already spread into nearby wood needs pest control as well.
Eastern subterranean termites are present across the state and more common in eastern Iowa than most homeowners expect. They are just far less visible than ants.

faqs.q: How close to my house is too close?
faqs.a: Inside 20 feet of a foundation or deck posts is worth removing. Inside 10 feet, treat it as a priority.

faqs.q: Do you have to remove the roots too?
faqs.a: Not usually. Buried roots rot underground without providing the open, above-grade nesting site that a standing stump does.
